newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe urged to handle labour with sensitivity.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe urged to handle labour with sensitivity.

text.p: Zimbabwe's main union boss urged President Robert Mugabe's government on Tuesday to handle labour issues with greater sensitivity this year, warning that a confrontational approach may revive labour unrest.

In an interview with Reuters, Morgan Tsvangirayi, secretary-general of the Zimbabwe Congress of Trade Unions (ZCTU), said his organisation would, like last year, be negotiating for annual wage rises well above the monthly average inflation rate.

"The economy is doing well almost all-round, and the wage talks shouldn't be that difficult. Except for the government which tried to play tough and was unreasonable in its approach, we had no difficulties last year," he said.
Tsvangirayi was referring to two unprecedented strikes by Zimbabwean civil servants over pay in 1996 which were both backed by the ZCTU.

In the first, which lasted for about three weeks in August, up to 80 percent of the southern African country's 180,000 civil servants demonstrated on the streets after rejecting wage increases of up to nine percent.
Although Mugabe's cash-strapped government had initially rejected their demands, it later bowed down and paid them an extra 20 percent.
A majority of state nurses and junior doctors walked out of their jobs again in October for two months, demanding wage rises of up to 60 percent and improved working conditions.
The government stood firm and a majority eventually returned to work empty-handed, save for promises that the government would look at their grievances.

"We are hoping the government will this year handle labour issues with more sensitivity. The arrogant and confrontational approach that we saw last year can only bring us strikes and unrest...and nobody wants that," Tsvangirayi said.
Zimbabwe's farm-based economy is expected to grow by up to seven percent this year, because of a good agricultural season, compared with estimated growth of five percent in 1996.
Wage rises averaged 30 percent in 1996 against an average monthly inflation rate of 21.7 percent. Many economists expect inflation to drop to between 16 and 18 percent this year.
Wage negotiations normally begin in March and are effective from July, the start of the government's financial year.

Tsvangirayi -- whose ZCTU represents about 200,000 of Zimbabwe's two million workers in the key mining, farming, tourism, energy, banking and manufacturing sectors -- said his organisation would be working at increasing its membership in 1997, and improving dialogue with the government and employers.
Florence Chitauro, the minister for public service, labour and social welfare told state media recently that the government was committed to regular communication with unions and industrialists.
